assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: Dedicated table 'Order Splitting — Fulfillment Method' with scenarios 'One delivery, one pickup' showing 2 shipments and 'Two delivery items, one pickup' showing separate shipments.

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: Dedicated table 'Order Splitting — Delivery Address' with scenarios 'Personal item + gift' and 'Three different addresses' showing separate shipments by address.

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: Dedicated table 'Order Splitting — Availability Window' with scenarios 'In stock + pre-order' showing separate timing (Shirt: now · Book: 2026-06-01).

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: Dedicated table 'Warehouse Allocation — Minimising Shipments' with scenario 'Two-warehouse solution preferred over three' showing minimization logic.

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: Dedicated table 'Companion Product Co-location' with scenarios showing pairs shipping together (Chicago: Camera body + Lens) when possible.

assertions.text: Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Fulfillment table includes 'All home delivery', 'All store pickup', and 'One delivery, one pickup' covering all three required scenarios.

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Delivery address table includes 'All to same address' and 'Personal item + gift' (different addresses) covering both required scenarios.

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates.
assertions.evidence: Availability table includes 'All in stock', 'In stock + pre-order', 'In stock + backorder (date unknown)', and 'Two different pre-order dates' covering all requirements.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: Warehouse table includes 'One warehouse covers full order', 'Two warehouses required, exact fit', 'Two-warehouse solution preferred over three', and 'Total stock insufficient'.

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: Table covers 'Shared warehouse available' (both in one warehouse) and 'No warehouse stocks both — forced split' (unavoidable split), but lacks scenario where one companion is unavailable anywhere.

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: All scenario names describe business situations: 'One delivery, one pickup', 'Two-warehouse solution preferred over three', 'Unavoidable split'.

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup}.
assertions.evidence: In fulfillment table, 'Shirt, Book' paired with 'Home Delivery, Store Pickup' uses ordered lists, not sets. Mapping is unambiguous: Shirt→Home Delivery, Book→Store Pickup.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Warehouse table uses 'Quantity' column with '6 shirts' (scalar), not item lists like [Shirt, Shirt, Shirt, ...].

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Column names: 'Shipments?', 'Delivery Addresses', 'Available Stock', 'Warehouses Used?', 'Companion Grouping?' — all business/domain language.

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: All output columns end with '?': 'Shipments?', 'Contents?', 'Shipment Timing?', 'Warehouses Used?', 'Companion Grouping?'.

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: In warehouse table, 'Two warehouses required, exact fit' assigns 4 shirts to Chicago (which has 4) and 2 to LA (which has 2), totaling 6 ordered.

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: Response includes dedicated 'Open Questions' section with 5 items plus inline question about tie-breaking in warehouse allocation scenarios.

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules.
assertions.evidence: Five separate tables: fulfillment method, delivery address, availability, warehouse allocation, and companion product co-location, each addressing one distinct concern.

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns.
assertions.evidence: Fulfillment table has 4 rows covering necessary combinations; companion table has 5 rows covering distinct co-location scenarios. No unnecessary permutations mixing concerns.
